1345.title: Kavishri, voice alone
1345.hook: unaccompanied sung poetry about Sikh history
1345.howItsDone: Kavishri groups sing Sikh history in fast, rhymed verse without instruments, one voice leading and the others joining, at gurdwara gatherings and fairs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dhadis, singing history with an hourglass drum and a fiddle. Your line was history sung.

Take away the drum. Take away the fiddle, the harmonium, the tabla. What's left? A few singers standing close together, one with a hand cupped by one ear, voices racing through verse at a speed that leaves the crowd breathless, rhymes landing like footsteps on a wooden floor. No instrument to lean on, nothing to hide behind. If a singer loses the beat, everybody hears it. This is sung poetry with nothing but the human voice, and it tells the same history the dhadis tell. Today's word is its name.
screen: `NO DRUM. NO FIDDLE.` → `VOICES RACING THROUGH VERSE.` → `NOTHING TO HIDE BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Kavishri is the art of the kavishar, the poet-singer. A kavishri group sings without instruments: one voice leads, the others answer and join, and the poetry itself carries the beat. Second, how a voice keeps time alone. Without a drum, the rhythm has to live inside the words. Kavishri verse is built in tight meters, with rhymes that come back on schedule, so the line drives itself forward. The singers breathe together, cut off together, and push the pace together: a kind of athletic poetry. Third, what it sings. Like the dhadis, kavishars sing the panth's history: the Gurus, the martyrs, the brave and the faithful, at gurdwara gatherings and at fairs where people come to remember. The story arrives fast, on bare breath. Fourth, why a bare voice is enough. The third pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, is a picture of people singing. In paraphrase: some sing of God's power, if they have the power to sing it; some sing of God's gifts, and know them as signs; some sing of God's glories and greatness; and still the telling never runs out. Each sings with whatever gift they were given; no one in that picture waits for the right equipment. A kavishar is a living version of that line: a poet, a breath, and a story worth telling, with nothing in the hands at all.

segments.voice: Say a few lines you know by heart out loud, slowly: a hymn, a verse from childhood, any poem that has stayed with you. Then say them again a little faster and find their beat with nothing but your own breath; if you'd rather stay silent, mouth the words, feel the rhythm in your chest, and sit in the quiet after the last line.
Kavishri. The art of the kavishar, the poet-singer: Sikh history sung fast and unaccompanied, with nothing but the voice. Today's word.
Your line: voice alone. When the beat lives in the words, the hands can stay empty. Until tomorrow.

1346.title: Katha traditions
1346.hook: different schools explain Gurbani in different styles
1346.howItsDone: In gurdwaras a giani may give katha after kirtan, explaining a line or hymn from the Guru Granth Sahib; explainers from different schools use word-by-word meaning, stories of the Gurus, or present-day examples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kavishri: Sikh history sung with nothing but the voice. Your line was voice alone.

The kirtan ends. The instruments are set aside, and someone sits facing the sangat with the scripture open nearby. No singing now, just talking. They take a single line sung a few minutes ago and open it: what each word means, which story it brings to mind, what it asks of a person on an ordinary Tuesday. At another gurdwara next week, someone will open the same line in a completely different way. Both are doing katha, explanation. Today is about the different traditions of doing it.
screen: `THE MUSIC STOPS. A VOICE BEGINS.` → `ONE LINE, OPENED UP.` → `NEXT WEEK, A DIFFERENT WAY.`

segments.voice: First, what katha is. The word means telling, or explanation. In a gurdwara, katha is the spoken part beside the sung part: a giani, a learned explainer, takes Gurbani and opens it for the sangat. Second, the styles. Some explainers go word by word, giving the meaning of each term and how it fits the grammar of the line. Some tell sakhis, stories from the lives of the Gurus, and let the story carry the meaning. Some draw on the vocabulary of older Indian philosophy, as the Nirmala and Udasi scholars did. Some trace their reading through a teaching lineage; the Damdami Taksal, for one, says its line of teachers goes back to Guru Gobind Singh. And some speakers today explain with history, science or everyday life, for listeners who grew up far from Punjab. Third, why there are many ways. In the sixteenth pauri of Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: if anyone tries to tell of it and reflect on it, there is no counting what the Creator has made. If the subject is that wide, no single explanation can finish it. Each school holds up a lamp to one part of a very large room. Fourth, how Sikhs hold the differences. Explainers sometimes disagree, and Sikhs argue about which readings are faithful; that argument is part of a living tradition. Above all of them sits the Guru Granth Sahib itself. The katha is a servant of the line, never its replacement.

Katha traditions. The schools and styles of explaining Gurbani aloud: word by word, through stories, through teaching lineages, through everyday life. Today's word.
Your line: many ways to explain. Many lamps, and the room is bigger than all of them. Rest well.

1347.title: Gurmat sangeet
1347.hook: schools teaching the ragas of the Granth
1347.howItsDone: Gurmat sangeet schools and teachers train students to sing kirtan in the ragas named in the Guru Granth Sahib, often on string instruments such as the rabab, saranda, taus and dilruba as well as the harmonium.

segments.voice: Yesterday, katha traditions, the many ways Gurbani is opened up aloud. Your line was many ways to explain.

A classroom with no desks. Students sit cross-legged on a rug, each with a long-necked string instrument resting against one shoulder, a bow in the other hand. The teacher sings a short phrase. The students play it back, a little ragged. The teacher sings it again, slower, bending one note just so. They try again. Down the hall, someone is practicing the same phrase alone, over and over. Nobody here is rehearsing for a concert. They're learning to sing scripture in the ragas its own headings name. Today's word is the name for that music.
screen: `A ROOM WITH NO DESKS.` → `THE TEACHER SINGS; THEY PLAY IT BACK.` → `SCRIPTURE, AS ITS HEADINGS ASK.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Gurmat means the Guru's way, the Guru's teaching; sangeet means music. Gurmat sangeet is the music of the Guru's way: kirtan sung in the ragas the Guru Granth Sahib names, with the care the book itself asks for. Second, why it needs schools. A raga isn't something you pick up from one hearing. Each has its own notes, its own climbing and falling, its own feeling, learned slowly at a teacher's feet. So schools and teachers keep raga kirtan alive, and pass it on student by student. Third, the instruments. Alongside the harmonium heard in gurdwaras today, these schools often teach the older string instruments: the rabab, the saranda, the taus, the dilruba. Some teachers say the strings can follow the bends of a raga's notes more closely. Others play the harmonium with great skill. Both are heard. Fourth, what the ragas carry. A raga has a mood, and Gurbani knows it. In a var in Raag Malar, the monsoon raga, Guru Amar Das says, in paraphrase: Malar is a cooling raga, and meditating on the Lord brings peace. Notice where the peace comes from: the raga sets the mood, and the remembering does the rest. That's what these schools keep: not music for its own sake, but a sound shaped to help the words land. When a student sings the Malar hymns in Malar, the music and the scripture speak together, under the heading the book gives them.

1348.title: Sikh painting
1348.hook: from miniature painters to modern artists like Sobha Singh
1348.howItsDone: Paintings of the Gurus and of Sikh history hang in homes, gurdwara halls and museums; Sikhs differ on how such pictures should be used, and they are not worshiped as the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmat sangeet, and Malar, the cooling raga. Your line was keeping the ragas.

A framed picture on the wall of a Punjabi living room. An old man with a white beard, eyes half closed, one hand raised in blessing, light gathering around his head. Grandparents walk past it every morning, and it's easy to grow up taking it as a likeness. But that face came from an artist's devotion and imagination. Behind that picture is a long line of painters who tried to put faith into color, from tiny miniatures to large modern canvases. Today's word is their work.
screen: `A PICTURE ON THE LIVING-ROOM WALL.` → `NOBODY PAINTED HIM FROM LIFE.` → `A LONG LINE OF PAINTERS.`

segments.voice: First, the small pictures. Illustrated janamsakhis, the life stories of Guru Nanak, show him in little scenes: under a tree, on a road with Mardana and his rabab, talking with holy men. Later, painters trained in the miniature styles of the Punjab hills worked for Sikh courts, painting rulers, Gurus and stories in fine detail with tiny brushes. Second, the modern canvas. In more recent times, painters like Sobha Singh made large, soft-lit portraits of the Gurus. His Guru Nanak, gentle and luminous, is the kind of picture that ends up framed in homes and gurdwara halls. Other modern artists paint the panth's history, its martyrs and Punjab's daily life, each in their own style. Third, an honest question. Since these faces come from devotion and imagination, each one is an artist's offering. Some Sikhs treasure these pictures as a way into devotion. Others are cautious, and ask that a painting never be bowed to or treated as the Guru, because for Sikhs the Guru today is the Guru Granth Sahib and the Word. Both are said with care. Fourth, what no paint can hold. The Mool Mantar, the opening of the Guru Granth Sahib, speaks of God as akaal moorat: in paraphrase, a form beyond time. A painting can show a Guru as an artist imagines him. It can't show the one the Guru pointed to. Maybe that's the gift these pictures can give: they point past themselves. Faith in paint, held lightly.

segments.voice: If you can, find a Sikh painting, a janamsakhi scene, a hill miniature or a modern portrait; if not, bring to mind any painting of someone holy to anyone. Let your eyes move slowly over the hands, the background, where the light falls, and ask what the painter chose to show and what they left out. Then let the picture point you past itself, toward whatever it was trying to honor.

1349.title: Sikh architecture
1349.hook: domes, small pavilions, pools and open doors
1349.howItsDone: Gurdwaras are built in different styles, from classic domed buildings with chhatris and a sarovar to converted local buildings; each flies the Nishan Sahib and keeps its doors and langar open to all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh painting, from janamsakhi scenes to Sobha Singh's portraits. Your line was faith in paint.

From the street, the first thing you see is the dome: rounded, ribbed like the petals of a closed lotus, with a gilded tip. Along the roofline, small open pavilions with their own little domes, like lanterns set out on a wall. Out front, a tall flagpole wrapped in cloth, a saffron flag at the top. Inside the gate, maybe a pool of still water, reflecting all of it. And the doors. Count them. Today's word is the way Sikhs build: what the shapes are, and what the doors are saying.
screen: `A RIBBED DOME, A GILDED TIP.` → `SMALL PAVILIONS ON THE ROOF.` → `AND THE DOORS.`

segments.voice: First, the shapes. Classic Sikh architecture draws on the building styles of its region and gives them its own accent: the ribbed dome, often called lotus-shaped; small domed pavilions, called chhatris, lining the roof; arched windows; gilded or white surfaces that catch the light. Outside stands the Nishan Sahib, the flagpole that tells a traveler from far off that a gurdwara is here. Second, the water. Some gurdwaras have a sarovar, a pool, where people may bathe or simply sit and look, and the building and its reflection become one picture. Third, the doors. Tradition says the Harmandir in Amritsar was built open on all four sides, and that this is the point: no side is the front door for one kind of person and the back door for another. Whoever comes, from whichever direction, walks straight in. Tradition also says the Harmandir sits lower than the ground around it, so everyone steps down to enter. Fourth, the line behind the doors. In Raag Suhi, Guru Arjan names the four classes of his society, the Kshatriya, the Brahmin, the Shudra and the Vaishya, and says, in paraphrase, that the teaching is shared by all four. Tradition reads the four doors as that line in brick and marble. A building can preach without saying a word: before you're even inside, it tells you who is welcome. A gurdwara in any style, in any country, is meant to say the same: the door is open, the kitchen is open, and nobody asks who you are.
screen: `RIBBED DOMES AND SMALL PAVILIONS.` · `A POOL THAT DOUBLES THE PICTURE.` · `DOORS ON ALL FOUR SIDES.` · `THE TEACHING IS SHARED BY ALL FOUR.` · then, large: `OPEN ON ALL SIDES.`

segments.voice: Think of a building you go into often, your home, your workplace, a place of worship, a shop, and notice its doors: which one guests use, and who might feel unwelcome at it. Don't fix anything; just see the doors clearly. Then picture a building with an open door on every side.
Sikh architecture. Ribbed domes, small rooftop pavilions, pools, a flag out front, and doors that say everyone may come in. Today's word.

1350.title: Phulkari, stitched flowers
1350.hook: Punjab's flower-embroidered shawls, made by women and given at weddings
1350.howItsDone: Phulkari shawls and baghs are embroidered by Punjabi women and brought out for weddings, births and celebrations; some families keep old ones as heirlooms, and the craft is still taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikh architecture: ribbed domes, still pools, and doors on every side. Your line was open on all sides.

A wedding morning in a Punjabi home. The bride sits very still while her mother lifts a heavy shawl out of a trunk and unfolds it over her shoulders. The cloth underneath is rough, hand-spun cotton, a deep red. But you can barely see it. Almost every inch is covered in silk thread, golden and orange and white, laid down in tiny straight stitches that catch the light and turn it into a field of flowers. Someone in the family made this, slowly, over a long time, for this morning. Today's word is that shawl.
screen: `A TRUNK OPENED ON A WEDDING MORNING.` → `ROUGH COTTON, BRIGHT SILK.` → `A FIELD OF FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: First, what it is. Phul is the Punjabi word for flower, and a phulkari is flower work: a shawl or head cloth embroidered in bright silk floss on hand-spun cotton. When the stitching covers the whole cloth, so the cotton disappears beneath it, people call it a bagh, a garden. Second, how it's made. Phulkari is worked largely from the back of the cloth, counting threads, in long darning stitches that lie flat and shine on the front. For some designs no pattern is drawn; it lives in the maker's head and hands. That's slow work, done in the gaps of a day, often with other women sitting close, talking. Third, what it carries. Phulkari belongs to Punjab's women across faiths, Sikh, Hindu and Muslim. Tradition in some families says a grandmother starts a bagh when a granddaughter is born, to give at her wedding. Whether or not a family keeps that custom, the shawl comes out at the big moments: weddings, births, celebrations. Fourth, why it sits in this path. In the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak speaks up for women. In paraphrase: why call her lesser, she from whom kings are born? A phulkari is women's work and women's wisdom, made by hand and handed down. It honors the ones who made it, the ones who wear it, and the long line between them: a story told without words, stitch by stitch.
screen: `PHUL: FLOWER. BAGH: A GARDEN.` · `WORKED FROM THE BACK, BY COUNT.` · `GIVEN AT WEDDINGS AND BIRTHS.` · `WHY CALL HER LESSER?` · then, large: `STITCHED FLOWERS.`

segments.voice: If there's stitched cloth near you, a cushion, a scarf, a hem, look at it close up and follow one thread with your eyes, noticing how many tiny decisions sit in a single flower. 1351.title: Sikh studies
1351.hook: universities around the world teach Sikh history and scripture
1351.howItsDone: Sikh studies is taught in universities in several countries, sometimes through chairs and programs Sikh communities helped fund; Sikh and non-Sikh scholars study Gurmukhi, scripture, history and the arts.

segments.voice: Yesterday, phulkari: silk flowers on hand-spun cotton, given at weddings. Your line was stitched flowers.

What happens when a scripture becomes a subject on a syllabus? On a gray afternoon in a lecture hall far from Punjab, a professor puts a page of Gurmukhi on the screen, and a room of students, some in turbans, some meeting the Gurus for the first time this term, lean in to work out a single line. Down the corridor, a graduate student is reading old manuscripts for a thesis. Universities far from Punjab, as well as in it, teach Sikh history and scripture. Today's word is that field.
screen: `A PAGE OF GURMUKHI ON THE SCREEN.` → `STUDENTS OF EVERY BACKGROUND.` → `A SHELF THAT KEEPS GROWING.`

segments.voice: First, what Sikh studies is: the academic study of the Sikh tradition, its scripture and languages, its history, its music and art, its life in Punjab and in every place Sikhs have settled. Students learn Gurmukhi, read the Guru Granth Sahib closely, and ask how the panth grew. Second, an early bridge. A British official named Max Arthur Macauliffe worked beside Sikh scholars, among them Bhai Kahn Singh of Nabha, to put the Gurus' hymns and lives into English, in a work called The Sikh Religion. He leaned on Sikh learning at every step, and this path still quotes his English in places. Third, an honest tension. Some Sikhs welcome study of their tradition, and some communities have helped fund chairs and programs. At times, though, a historian's reading of a manuscript or a story has unsettled Sikhs who hold a different understanding, and there have been real arguments. Sikh scholars work inside the universities too, holding faith and research together. Both trust and caution are part of the story. Fourth, what Guru Nanak said about reading. In the Asa di Var he pictures someone reading cartloads of books, reading for months and years, all through life. And then, in paraphrase: only one thing is of account; the rest is the chatter of ego. Some readers take that one thing as the Name. Study can serve it, or it can get in the way.
